cards.text: Asaph, the psalm's writer, is still walking his people back through their history so the next generation won't forget. And he's not done with the wilderness yet. He says how often they disobeyed God there and grieved Him in the desert.

cards.question: True or false: Asaph says Israel tested God only once in the wilderness.

cards.text: So how does a people keep doing that? Asaph points straight at something they let slip their minds.

cards.question: What does Asaph say Israel did not remember?

answers.text: God's power the day He redeemed them
The names of their fathers' tribes
The road that led back to Egypt

cards.text: Then Asaph rewinds all the way to God's signs in Egypt and His wonders in the fields of Zoan. He is scrolling WAY back in the group chat, friend.

cards.question: Asaph starts with Egypt's rivers. What did God turn them into?

cards.text: Next God sends swarms of flies that devoured them, and frogs that devastated them. One frog hops out of my oven and I'm on the CEILING, friend. Gold base and all.

cards.question: Then God goes after the crops of Egypt. What did He give them to?
True or false: In Egypt the hail struck both the vines and the cattle.

cards.text: Then God unleashes His fury on Egypt, a band of destroying angels. He clears a path for His anger and does not spare them from death.

cards.question: Who in Egypt does Asaph say God struck?

cards.text: Now the picture changes. Asaph turns from what God did to Egypt to how God brought His own people out.

cards.question: How does Asaph say God led His people out into the wilderness?
God led Israel safely so they did not fear. What happened to their enemies?

cards.text: And God doesn't drop them off halfway. He brings them all the way to His holy land, to the mountain His right hand had acquired. Door to door, friend. No "you can walk from here."

cards.question: God drove out nations before Israel and gave the tribes their ___.

cards.text: Land settled, tents up. Happy ending? Nope. They tested and disobeyed God Most High and turned back, faithless like their fathers.

cards.question: Asaph compares Israel to a weapon that can't be trusted. Which one?

cards.text: They enraged Him with their high places. That's me and my oven timer: it saves my batch every single time, and every single time I ignore it AGAIN.

cards.question: What did Israel provoke God's jealousy with?

cards.text: On hearing it, God was furious and rejected Israel completely.

cards.question: Then God abandoned the tent He had pitched among men. Where was it?

cards.text: He delivered His strength to captivity, and His splendor to the hand of the adversary.

cards.question: Asaph says God surrendered His people to the sword. What reason does he give?

answers.text: He was enraged by His heritage
He wanted to test their strength
They had asked Him for a king

cards.text: It gets heavy. Fire consumed His young men and their maidens were left without wedding songs. Then the sword reaches His priests.

cards.question: True or false: The priests' widows led the mourning for them.

cards.text: Then everything turns. The Lord awoke as from sleep, like a mighty warrior overcome by wine.

cards.question: Once the Lord rises up like a mighty warrior, what does He do?

cards.text: But He doesn't go back to the old setup. He rejected the tent of Joseph and refused the tribe of Ephraim.

cards.question: God refused the tribe of Ephraim. Which tribe did He choose instead?
Along with Judah, God chose Mount ___, which He loved.

cards.text: He built His sanctuary like the heights, like the earth He has established forever.

cards.question: Then God chose David His servant. Where did God take David from?
David went from tending the ewes to what new job for God's people?

cards.text: So David shepherded them with integrity of heart and guided them with skillful hands. God led His people out like sheep, and now He hands that flock to a shepherd.

findings.problem: The card says Asaph is walking back through history "so the next generation won't forget." That fact comes from Psalm 78:4-6, which is outside this passage, and it has no reference. The card cites only Psalm 78:40.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: The setup says "how often they disobeyed God there." That already rules out the idea in card 2 that Israel tested God only once. Verse 40 and verse 41 say the same thing in parallel, so the true or false answer is given away.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: "So how does a people keep doing that? Asaph points straight at something they let slip their minds" presents verse 42's forgetting as the cause of verse 41's testing. The text puts the two lines side by side but doesn't say one causes the other.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: This is a which-thing question, but the wrong answers "Sand" and "Salt water" aren't real details of God turning water into something anywhere in the Bible.

rule.text: For who, which thing and where questions, wrong answers are real details from somewhere in the Bible, like Joppa when the right answer is Tarshish.

findings.problem: The story card has 4 sentences ("Land settled, tents up." / "Happy ending?" / "Nope." / "They tested...").

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: "Land settled, tents up" uses Psalm 78:55 ("settled the tribes of Israel in their tents"), but the card cites only Psalm 78:56-57.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The question asks which weapon, but "A cracked shield" is armor, not a weapon. It isn't the same kind of thing as the other answers.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone.

findings.problem: The joke sets "They enraged Him with their high places" next to ignoring an oven timer that keeps saving his batch. The fact's action is provoking God with high places. The comparison's action is ignoring something helpful over and over. The actions don't match, so the line doesn't click.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The story card is the verse word for word, with no Papa Dorin voice and no context.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The story card is the verse word for word, with no Papa Dorin voice and no context. A baker can't tell what the moment means.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The right answer, "He was enraged by His heritage," uses the BSB's own Bible-sounding wording. The wrong answers are plain modern phrasing, so the right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.
Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: "Once the Lord rises up like a mighty warrior" changes the text's simile. Psalm 78:65 says He "awoke as from sleep, like a mighty warrior overcome by wine." "Rises up" isn't in the text, and the card drops "overcome by wine."
"But He doesn't go back to the old setup" ties the rejection of Joseph and Ephraim to Shiloh and what came before. The text doesn't make that connection.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The story card is the verse word for word, with no Papa Dorin voice and no context.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: Psalm 78:61 ("He delivered His strength to captivity, and His splendor to the hand of the adversary") is hard to follow without knowing it is widely read as the ark's capture in 1 Samuel 4. The psalm itself never names the ark. The rules say to leave open what the text leaves open and to connect passages only by what the texts state. They also say a story card needs enough context that the moment makes sense.
findings.question: Can Papa Dorin tell the baker that "His strength" and "His splendor" point to the ark being captured, with a reference like 1 Samuel 4:11? Or must the card leave it unexplained and rely only on a dictionary or idiom pop-up?
